presentingComplaint: Progressive drowsiness, unresponsiveness and feeling intensely cold over 3 days in a woman with known alcohol-related cirrhosis.
history: Known Child-Pugh B alcohol-related cirrhosis (2 prior admissions with ascites) and long-standing primary hypothyroidism after radioactive iodine for Graves' disease 15 years ago. Family report she stopped her levothyroxine ~6 weeks ago because she 'ran out' and could not attend clinic. Over the past week she became increasingly lethargic, constipated and cold-intolerant, then over 3 days confused and finally difficult to rouse. A grandchild had a coryzal illness the week before. No paracetamol or benzodiazepine overdose; her only medication otherwise is spironolactone. Presentation is winter. The team initially considered decompensated cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy given her asterixis, jaundice and ascites, but the profound hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and non-pitting oedema pointed to a thyroid emergency.
examination: Obtunded (GCS 8, E2 V2 M4), not localising, responding only to pain. Cold peripheries with core temperature 32.4°C. Coarse dry skin, periorbital puffiness and non-pitting oedema of the shins and hands. Sparse eyebrows, hoarse-sounding groans, delayed relaxation of ankle jerks. Mild scleral icterus and shifting dullness with moderate ascites. Asterixis elicited before she became too drowsy to sustain posture. Chest clear; heart sounds slow and quiet with no murmur. No focal neurological deficit, neck supple.

labs.abg: pH 7.29, pCO2 7.8 kPa, pO2 8.4 kPa (type 2 respiratory failure with hypercapnia)

imaging: CXR: low lung volumes, small bilateral pleural effusions, no consolidation. CT head: age-appropriate atrophy, no haemorrhage or mass. USS abdomen: coarse nodular cirrhotic liver with moderate ascites, patent portal vein.
microbiology: Blood cultures, urine culture and diagnostic ascitic tap sent to exclude a precipitating infection/SBP; ascitic PMN 90 cells/µL (below 250 threshold — no SBP). Cultures pending and no organism isolated at 48h.
differentialDiagnoses: Myxoedema coma (decompensated primary hypothyroidism precipitated by levothyroxine cessation, cold exposure and viral illness)
finalDiagnosis: Myxoedema coma — decompensated primary hypothyroidism (post-radioiodine) precipitated by levothyroxine non-adherence, hypothermia and intercurrent viral illness, with overlapping decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis confounding the picture.
citations: American Thyroid Association — Guidelines for the Treatment of Hypothyroidism, 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Hypothyroidism and Myxedema Coma
stewardship: No antimicrobial indicated for the primary diagnosis; myxoedema coma is non-infective. Because infection is a common precipitant and the picture overlaps with cirrhosis/SBP, cultures and a diagnostic ascitic tap were taken and empiric antibiotics were considered but withheld once SBP was excluded (ascitic PMN <250) and cultures remained negative. Definitive treatment is IV levothyroxine (loading dose) plus/minus liothyronine, empiric IV hydrocortisone until coexisting adrenal insufficiency is excluded, passive rewarming, and correction of hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia in a critical-care setting.
contraindications: Rapid correction of hyponatraemia (>8-10 mmol/L per 24h) risks osmotic demyelination — correct slowly
Active external rewarming can precipitate vasodilatory shock — use passive rewarming
Do not give levothyroxine before empiric hydrocortisone if adrenal insufficiency not excluded (risk of precipitating adrenal crisis)
Caution with sedatives/opioids given hypoventilation, hepatic impairment and reduced drug clearance in cirrhosis
edgeCases: Cirrhosis-related asterixis, jaundice, ascites and hyperammonaemia mimic hepatic encephalopathy and can mask the thyroid emergency
Sick-euthyroid changes in cirrhosis can blunt free T4, but a markedly elevated TSH with very low free T4 confirms true primary hypothyroidism
Hypothermia may falsely normalise a septic temperature; a low reading thermometer is needed
Coexisting Graves'/autoimmune history raises the chance of concurrent primary adrenal insufficiency (Schmidt syndrome) — check cortisol
expectedNextQuestions: Is she adherent with levothyroxine and when was the last dose?
Any prior thyroid surgery, radioiodine or neck irradiation?
Any precipitant — cold exposure, infection, sedatives, recent illness?
Baseline mental state and whether asterixis/jaundice are chronic from her cirrhosis?
expectedInvestigations: TSH and free T4 (and free T3)
Random/short synacthen cortisol before steroid cover
Serum sodium, glucose, creatinine and venous/arterial blood gas for CO2 retention
Septic screen including diagnostic ascitic tap (cell count + culture), blood and urine cultures
ECG (bradycardia, low voltage, prolonged QT) and CT head to exclude structural cause

investigations: Septic screen with diagnostic ascitic tap

regressionAssertions: Engine must rank myxedema as the top diagnosis despite cirrhosis confounders (asterixis, jaundice, ascites)
Markedly elevated TSH with very low free T4 must drive the diagnosis over hepatic_enceph
No antibiotics should be recommended once SBP is excluded and cultures are negative
Empiric IV hydrocortisone must be advised before/with levothyroxine until adrenal insufficiency excluded
Hyponatraemia correction must be flagged as slow to avoid osmotic demyelination
